source: Robinson (1965) A machine-oriented logic based on the resolution principle, J. ACM 12(1):23-41
finding: Robinson made one inference rule (resolution) with a most general unifier, replacing Davis-Putnam (1960) enumeration of ground instances. Not read first-hand; facts come from the Wikipedia summary (item a02).
numbers: Journal pages 23-41, vol 12 no 1. Davis-Putnam 1960 needed all ground instances.
limits: Paper itself not opened; secondhand only.
agent_relevance: The core move is: unify first, then infer. The lesson for our agent is that a good representation removes blind enumeration.

source: Wikipedia: Resolution (logic)
finding: Resolution is sound and refutation complete for propositional and first-order logic. With factoring added, a clause set is unsatisfiable iff the empty clause is derivable. Without factoring a worked example never reaches the empty clause; with it, 7 steps.
numbers: Example: 7-step derivation with factoring. Davis-Putnam rule on p.210. Lists Otter, SPASS, Vampire, Prover9 among implementations.
limits: Secondary summary. Page does not mention given clause or Haken lower bounds (checked).
agent_relevance: Completeness is for refutation: assume the negation and look for contradiction. A template for a try-to-break-it check, used as a check, not a vote (G3).

source: Wikipedia: Superposition calculus
finding: Superposition (Bachmair and Ganzinger, J. Logic and Computation 3(4), 1994) merges resolution with ordered Knuth-Bendix completion for equality. It is refutation complete under a fair derivation strategy. E, SPASS, Vampire and Waldmeister are built on it.
numbers: Bachmair-Ganzinger 1994 JLC 3(4); Nieuwenhuis-Rubio 2001 Handbook chapter.
limits: Primary paper not opened. Page has no detail on redundancy or ordering conditions.
agent_relevance: Fairness is the key condition: every possible inference must eventually be chosen. A scaffold that prunes by a score needs a fairness floor so no branch starves forever.

source: Wikipedia: Otter (theorem prover)
finding: Otter (McCune, Argonne) was the first widely distributed high-performance first-order prover. It uses resolution, paramodulation, hyperresolution, set of support, a given-clause loop, and efficient term indexing. Successor is Prover9.
numbers: About 28,000 lines of C (Wos and Pieper 1999). Last change 14 Sep 2004. McCune 1992 indexing paper; McCune and Wos 1997 CADE-13 paper.
limits: Page gives no search results and no Robbins result.
agent_relevance: The given-clause loop (pick one clause, combine with all kept clauses) is the unit of control the whole field tunes.

source: Wikipedia: Robbins algebra
finding: McCune's EQP (an equational prover, not general Otter) proved the Robbins conjecture in 1996-97. Huntington, Robbins and Tarski had failed by hand since the 1930s.
numbers: Proof took 8 days. Robbins was 81 when told. Dahn simplified the proof in 1998.
limits: Page is inconsistent on 1996 vs 1997. A tailor-made prototype for this one problem.
agent_relevance: A saturation run can settle a famous open question, but only with a specialised prover and days of compute. Heavy search is for few problems; plan a budget.

source: Wikipedia: Vampire (theorem prover)
finding: Vampire (Voronkov, Riazanov, Hoder, Kovacs, Reger, Suda) implements ordered binary resolution and superposition with splitting, subsumption, KBO ordering, indexing and proof output.
numbers: At least 53 CASC trophies since 1999. Release 4.5.1 on 2020-07-15. Written in C++.
limits: No per-year breakdown; omits AVATAR.
agent_relevance: One prover with many tuned strategies keeps winning: strategy diversity matters more than one clever rule.

source: Wikipedia: E (theorem prover)
finding: E (Schulz) is an equational superposition prover with shared term rewriting, literal selection and ML-based search guidance. It is part of Isabelle Sledgehammer.
numbers: CASC: won CNF/MIX 2000; 2nd 2008; 2nd in FOF and UEQ 2009; overall best special award 2010; won CNF 2011.
limits: Start year not given; Schulz AICOM 2002 is the earliest reference.
agent_relevance: Open-source E is the main test bed for learned clause selection (items a12 to a22).

source: Kovacs and Voronkov (2013) First-Order Theorem Proving and Vampire, CAV 2013 (saturation and fairness)
finding: A saturation algorithm picks an inference, applies it, adds the result, and must be fair or completeness is lost. Three outcomes: empty clause found, saturation ends (satisfiable), or it runs forever.
numbers: Vampire 2.6: first version 1993; about 152,000 SLOC; 27 CASC wins including two titles in 2012.
limits: Describes Vampire 2.6 only; later versions differ.
agent_relevance: Select, infer, simplify, repeat, with a fairness rule. The program (not the model) decides each transition, matching section 1 of the schema.
quote: A saturation algorithm with a fair inference selection strategy is called a fair saturation algorithm.

source: Kovacs and Voronkov (2013) clause selection by age and weight
finding: Default clause selection mixes two priority queues: oldest clause and lightest clause (weight = symbol count). With ratio (a,w), of each a+w picks, a come by age and w by weight.
numbers: Example: ratio 2:3 means 2 of every 5 picks by age, 3 by weight.
limits: Hand-set ratio; no learning. The weight test can drop non-redundant clauses, so Vampire then never answers 'satisfiable'.
agent_relevance: A cheap blend of breadth-first (age) and best-first (weight). Direct analogue: expand the oldest open branch some of the time and the most promising the rest, at a fixed ratio chosen by code.

source: Kovacs and Voronkov (2013) Otter vs Discount loops, limited resource strategy
finding: Otter loop lets unselected (passive) clauses simplify others; kept clauses then pile up and slow processing. Vampire's default limited resource strategy (LRS) estimates from time per given clause which passive clauses cannot be reached before the time limit and drops them.
numbers: No numeric benchmark in this section.
limits: LRS is incomplete by design and works only with a time limit. Authors call dropped clauses 'unreachable', not 'redundant'.
agent_relevance: Strong analogue for budgeted search: drop branches that cannot be reached in the remaining budget, using arithmetic on measured speed, not model opinion.
quote: unreachability is fundamentally different from redundancy

source: Gleiss and Suda (2020) Layered Clause Selection for Saturation-Based Theorem Proving, CEUR 2752
finding: Layered selection groups clauses by a numeric feature (theory content, goal distance, AVATAR split dependencies, closeness to Horn) and alternates between groups, with age-weight inside each group. On TPTP all four new features beat the base; on SMTLIB one (av) did worse than base.
numbers: TPTP: base about 9,108 to 9,204 solved; new heuristics 9,160 / 9,289 / 9,525 / 9,526; union of all four 10,297 (+1,189 over base). SMTLIB base about 39,943 to 41,841; union gain 3,226.
limits: Table 2 text extraction was partly garbled, so row-to-label mapping is approximate. Authors say repeated runs vary (9,512 vs 9,525 for the default) because LRS is timing sensitive.
agent_relevance: Even a hand-built feature split gives large gains; the union of differently-biased strategies beats any single one. Supports running several selection biases and taking the union.

source: Loos, Irving, Szegedy, Kaliszyk (2017) Deep Network Guided Proof Search, LPAR-21
finding: First deep nets (CNN, WaveNet) choosing the next given clause inside E, trained on 91,877 Mizar proofs. A pure net did badly; a hybrid alternating net and E's Auto heuristic did better; the best was a two-phase switch (net-guided 20 min, then Auto 10 min).
numbers: Mizar FOL: 57,882 theorems, 32,521 (56%) with an ATP proof. Train 82,718 proofs / 29,325 conjectures; holdout 3,196 conjectures, 9,159 proofs. Holdout proved within 1,000 processed clauses: Auto 89.0%, WaveNet 640* 91.4%, WaveNet 256 92.3%; at 10,000: Auto 94.3% vs 95.5-95.7%. Hard set of 25,361 theorems: new proofs for 7.36% (1,866); corpus coverage 56% to 59%.
limits: Nets are slow, so gains show per processed clause, not per second, without the switch. More accurate WaveNets (79.9-81.5% clause accuracy) guided worse than simple CNNs. Auto already solves 96.6% of the holdout.
agent_relevance: An expensive learned scorer helps most when mixed with a cheap fixed rule and handed off to it as the budget runs out. Scorer accuracy did not predict search help.
quote: neural network guidance is still too slow on current hardware

source: Loos et al. (2017) two-phase finding
finding: Without the second, fast-heuristic phase, network-guided search often processes only 1% of the clauses a fast-heuristic search would. The slow phase is worth it only because it sets up a better starting point.
numbers: Net phase 20 minutes, then Auto 10 minutes, for every reported run.
limits: Fixed time split chosen by the authors; no sweep of the split reported in the text I read.
agent_relevance: Spend slow, smart effort early, then switch to cheap breadth when time is short. A budget-split rule the program can enforce.

source: Jakubuv and Urban (2017) ENIGMA: Efficient Learning-based Inference Guiding Machine
finding: A fast linear classifier (LIBLINEAR, term and symbol features) learned from past E proofs scores clauses; E mixes it with normal weights at set frequencies. On CASC 2016 AIM it beat a strong E strategy and Vampire.
numbers: AIM: 1020 training problems; strategy S0 solved 239 in 30 s (auto-schedule 261); classifier-guided runs solved 337 train problems. Competition 200 problems at 180 s: S0 22, best mixed (frequency 30, eps 0.2) 41, all strategies 52 vs Vampire 47 (3x180 s). Boosting positives 10x raised positive-class accuracy 12.5% to 81.8% (overall 98% to 93%); result 57 solved, 16 unsolved by Vampire.
limits: One benchmark family (AIM, algebra); test resembles training. Competition numbers come from many strategy variants, so partly tuned.
agent_relevance: A cheap learner trained on the system's own solved cases, plus a retrain loop and a class-imbalance fix, gave big gains. No bigger model needed.

source: Jakubuv and Urban (2017) ENIGMA classifier speed
finding: Learning takes seconds and scoring takes about 10 microseconds per clause, comparable to the rate at which E generates clauses, so ordinary users can train it without a long training phase.
numbers: Classifier M1 trained in about 7 s on 6,821 positive and 219,012 negative examples; 97.6% accuracy on the training examples (M0).
limits: Accuracy is on training data; ratio of positives to negatives is about 1 to 32.
agent_relevance: Scoring cost must be about the same as the cost of generating a candidate, or the scorer becomes the bottleneck.

source: Jakubuv and Urban (2019) Hammering Mizar by Learning Clause Guidance, ITP 2019
finding: ENIGMA with gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost, 200 trees) and looped retraining on the whole Mizar library. Single strategy improved 70% in real time.
numbers: Mizar problems solved in 10 s: baseline 14,933; best looped strategy 25,397 (+70.0%, depth-16 trees). At 60 s: 26,107 vs 22,068 for the old 6-strategy portfolio (+18.3%); Vampire CASC portfolio at 300 s solved 27,842.
limits: Gain shrinks at longer time and against portfolios. Trained and tested on Mizar, so no transfer claim.
agent_relevance: Looping (retrain on what the last guided run solved) kept adding problems each round. A scaffold that logs solved cases and reweights toward their patterns has a precedent, with the transfer caveat (a22).

source: Jakubuv and Urban (2019) ENIGMA-NG: Efficient Neural and Gradient-Boosted Inference Guidance for E, CICM 2019
finding: Compared linear, tree and recursive-neural clause scorers on MPTP2078 at 10 s per problem. Trees won in real time; the neural model was the slowest per clause but cut given-clause steps as much.
numbers: Baseline S solved 1086 of 2078. Variants solved 1115, 1210, 1231, 1256 (best tree mix), 1167, 1197 (neural). Best is +15.7% over S and +3.8% over the best linear. Clause evaluation speed: linear about 60% of E, trees about 40%, neural 6-7% (3.6% without caching). 232 newly solved problems; TPR and TNR fall about 15% and 20% on them.
limits: Column labels in extraction were garbled; 1256 and 15.7% are in the text. Accuracy drop on newly solved problems signals generalisation limits.
agent_relevance: Faster scorer wins in wall-clock even if less expressive. Report cost per scoring call, not only accuracy.

source: Jakubuv, Chvalovsky, Olsak, Piotrowski, Suda, Urban (2020) ENIGMA Anonymous: Symbol-Independent Inference Guiding Machine, IJCAR 2020
finding: Made clause scoring independent of symbol names (arity-based features, symbol-independent GNNs), with GNN scoring batched against a context of already selected clauses. Boosted trees overtook GNNs in later loop iterations.
numbers: 10 s: baseline 14,966; D2 (LightGBM) 24,347 (+62.7%); N2 (GNN) 23,262 (+55.4%). Abstract-time (5,000 generated clauses): baseline 10,679; D2 22,661 (+112.2%); N2 22,169 (+107.6%). Twenty strategies together solved 2,109 Mizar40 hard problems that no earlier method solved (200 s).
limits: Same library for training and testing. GNN N2 training took 1 day 8 hours vs 40 min for D2.
agent_relevance: Symbol independence is what lets a guide transfer. Our features should describe structure (size, depth, relation to goal), not names.

source: Chvalovsky, Jakubuv, Olsak, Urban (2021) Learning Theorem Proving Components, TABLEAUX 2021
finding: Extends the context idea: choose the next given clause by its fit with learned components (clusters of related clauses) of the clause graph, not by the clause alone.
numbers: Only abstract and introduction read; intro cites 73.5% of Mizar theorems (over 40k) as automatically provable.
limits: Experimental tables not read in this pass.
agent_relevance: Judge a candidate relative to what is already chosen. Same idea as diversity-aware selection.

source: Suda (2021) Improving ENIGMA-Style Clause Selection While Learning From History, CADE-28
finding: Vampire guided by a recursive neural network over derivation history (flagging theory axioms) gets a 41% gain on a relevant SMT-LIB subset in real time. Mixes with the stock rule win; net-only versions are weak.
numbers: Table (partly garbled): stock S 756 solved; the best mix of S with the history-trained net at a 1:2 ratio solved 1,036 (137% of S). Pure net variants: 55 and 190 solved. Abstract states 41%.
limits: 41% is from the abstract; 37% (1036/756) is my reading of the table row. Table text was garbled, so row labels are uncertain.
agent_relevance: The net alone scored far below the stock rule; mixes won. Keep a fixed fallback when a learned scorer picks.

source: Crouse et al. (2020) A Deep Reinforcement Learning Approach to First-Order Logic Theorem Proving (TRAIL), AAAI 2021
finding: TRAIL trains an attention-based policy to pick inferences in a saturation prover (Beagle) from a random start over 10 iterations of self-generated data. It beats other RL provers but still loses to E.
numbers: Solved on M2k / MPTP2078: E 1922/998; Beagle 1543/742; mlCop 1034/502; rlCop 1235/733; plCop 1359/782; TRAIL 1561/910. TRAIL is +202 and +128 over plCop and +22% over Beagle on MPTP2078. Limit 2,000 steps and 100 s. Transfer: 11% loss training on MPTP and testing on M2k, 3% the other way.
limits: Reports the best iteration (a selection effect). E is best on both sets. Row-to-system mapping reconstructed from the text differences (202, 128, 22%).
agent_relevance: Learned search from scratch has not beaten hand-engineered E. Best-iteration reporting must be matched to a held-out check (G3).

source: Chvalovsky, Suda, Urban (2026) Teaching Vampire New Tricks: An Experimental Study of Neural Clause Selection, arXiv 2609.16228
finding: Tests neural clause selection (graph model trained iteratively on proof traces inside Vampire) on four sets. Gains are large inside a dataset, but a model trained on one dataset scores below the plain default on the others. One model trained on all sets almost recovers.
numbers: Vampire default, 32 billion instruction limit (about 12 s). Default to boosted: TPTP 8,511 to 10,864 (+27.6%, 15,500 problems); Mizar40 test 1,543 to 3,101 (+101.0%); Isabelle test 2,178 to 2,715 (+24.7%); CoqHammer test 399 to 772 (+93.5%; train +248.3%). Combined model reaches 100.0% / 99.4% / 101.4% / 95.3% of the dedicated models.
limits: Cross-dataset transfer fails; the TPTP model beat default on Mizar40 only because TPTP holds 1,840 Mizar problems, and it fell below default once these were removed (TPTP-noMizar). The CoqHammer split by separate packages shows a smaller test than train gain.
agent_relevance: A real failed-transfer result. Guidance learned on one distribution can be worse than none elsewhere. Train on a mix and test on held-out families.

source: Chvalovsky, Suda, Urban (2026) portfolio experiments, arXiv 2609.16228
finding: Five baseline strategies chosen by greedy cover were each boosted by a trained model. The boost shrinks when strategies are combined, because neural guidance replaces the age-weight options that made strategies differ.
numbers: Per-strategy boost average 24.0%; 5-strategy portfolio +13.9%; one model for all five average +23.8%, covering 12,195 problems. Default 8,574 vs strategy 1 at 9,265. Champion gained 15.7% from the other four unboosted but only 8.4% once boosted. Schedule covers 4.1% more problems overall and 12.2% more at 10 s (76.1% vs 67.8%).
limits: Authors call the picture under combined strategies less clear-cut, with diminishing returns.
agent_relevance: Learned selection and strategy diversity overlap: each helps less when the other is present. Do not add assumed gains.

source: Piepenbrock, Urban, Korovin, Olsak, Heskes, Janota (2022) Machine Learning Meets The Herbrand Universe
finding: A different route: ML proposes ground instances (Herbrand instantiation) that a SAT solver then checks, rather than guiding the clause loop. Described as the first ML system for this task (GNN to RNN design).
numbers: Only abstract and intro read; no figures taken.
limits: No result numbers recorded.
agent_relevance: Alternative to saturation: guess instances, then check with a fast propositional solver. Links to the SAT subfield (02).

source: Pan, Albalak, Wang, Wang (2023) Logic-LM: Empowering LLMs with Symbolic Solvers for Faithful Logical Reasoning
finding: LLM translates a word problem to first-order logic and Prover9 (CNF plus resolution, Robinson 1965) decides. Un-executable cases fall back to chain of thought. Self-refinement from solver error messages added accuracy.
numbers: GPT-4 accuracy, standard / CoT / Logic-LM: ProofWriter 52.67 / 68.11 / 79.66; FOLIO 69.11 / 70.58 / 78.92; PrOntoQA 77.40 / 98.79 / 83.20; LogicalDeduction 71.33 / 75.25 / 87.63; AR-LSAT 33.33 / 35.06 / 43.04. Average gain +39.2% over standard and +18.4% over CoT (GPT-3.5 average). FOLIO executable rate for GPT-3.5: 66.7% before, 84.3% after refinement.
limits: On PrOntoQA GPT-4 CoT (98.79) beat Logic-LM (83.20). Errors come from translation, not the prover. Which base model the averages use is as stated in the paper.
agent_relevance: Using a resolution prover as an external checker turns the LLM into a translator and removes inference errors. Matches G2 and G3: real solver output to revise from.

source: Olausson et al. (2023) LINC: Logical Inference via Neurosymbolic Computation, EMNLP 2023
finding: LLM parses premises and conclusion to first-order logic several times, Prover9 evaluates each parse, and a majority vote picks the label. Large gains on a balanced ProofWriter subset; on FOLIO GPT-4 is about equal to chain of thought, and the two fail in different ways.
numbers: StarCoder+ (15.5B) with LINC beats GPT-3.5 CoT by 38 and GPT-4 CoT by 10 points on ProofWriter. GPT-4 with LINC is 26 points above CoT on ProofWriter. StarCoder+ FOLIO mean accuracy is 14.2 points above controls.
limits: FOLIO is in-distribution for the few-shot prompts; ProofWriter is out of distribution. Most losses are translation faults. Voting over samples from one model is the G4 hazard.
agent_relevance: A resolution prover as verifier works, and LLM-plus-prover and LLM-alone errors are complementary. Sampled parses are correlated, so agreement is a hint only.
